summary: This module covers the fundamentals, system architecture, operational subsystems, and practical applications of Diesel Power Plants. It details the working principle of the diesel prime mover, where burning fuel creates high temperatures (1500°C to 2000°C) and pressures to drive reciprocating pistons that turn the generator shaft. The module thoroughly analyzes the five core auxiliary systems: (i) Fuel supply system (bulk tank, filter, day tank, injectors), (ii) Air intake system (air filter), (iii) Exhaust system (silencer), (iv) Cooling system (water jackets, heat exchanger, cooling tower), and (v) Lubricating system (oil tank, oil pump, oil cooler). Finally, it contrasts the key advantages (simple design, less space, limited cooling water, 150 MW efficiency, quick start, no ash handling, less supervision) with disadvantages (high maintenance and lubrication costs, expensive diesel fuel, higher plant cost per kW, shorter plant life, noise, limited scale) and outlines their practical utility.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What is a Diesel Power Plant? State its basic working principle.
sa.a:
A Diesel Power Plant is a power generating station that uses a diesel engine as prime mover coupled to an AC generator (alternator).

Working Principle: When the diesel fuel burns inside the engine cylinder, it starts to produce mechanical power. The combustion of diesel fuel produces increased temperature (1500°C to 2000°C) and pressure inside the engine. Due to this pressure, gases are formed; this gas pushes the piston inside the diesel engine, producing mechanical power that rotates the shaft of the diesel engine and spins the generator.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): List the major auxiliary systems of an industrial diesel power plant.
sa.a:
The five essential auxiliary systems of a diesel power plant are:
(i) Fuel supply system
(ii) Air intake system
(iii) Exhaust system
(iv) Cooling system
(v) Lubricating system
(Together with the Diesel Engine and AC Generator/Alternator).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Explain the purpose and functioning of the All-Day fuel tank in a diesel power plant.
sa.a:
(i) Fuel Supply System:
Fuel from the storage tank is pumped through a filter into a smaller tank called the all-day tank. This tank supplies the daily requirements of the diesel engine.

(ii) Functioning: The all-day tank is placed at an elevated level to feed fuel to the engine injection system by gravity flow, and an overflow pipe returns excess fuel back to the bulk tank.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): How are large industrial diesel engines started in a power plant?
sa.a:
Large diesel engines in power plants are started using a Compressed Air Starting System:
(i) An air compressor charges high-pressure air into an air tank.
(ii) High-pressure air is admitted through starting valves into the engine cylinders to crank the crankshaft.
(iii) Once the engine reaches firing speed, fuel injection begins and the engine continues rotating on fuel combustion.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State any four major advantages of a diesel power plant.
sa.a:
Advantages of a diesel power plant include:
(i) Very simple design, simple installation, and occupies less space.
(ii) Limited cooling water requirement.
(iii) Diesel power plants are more efficient than steam power in the range of 150 MW capacity.
(iv) Quickly started and put on load; responds to varying loads without difficulty.
(v) Smaller storage needed for fuel; layout of power plant is quite simple.
(vi) There is no problem of ash handling, and less supervision is required.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State any four limitations or disadvantages of a diesel power plant.
sa.a:
Disadvantages of a diesel power plant include:
(i) High maintenance, lubrication cost, and operating cost.
(ii) Fuel cost is more, since in India diesel is costly.
(iii) The plant cost per kW is comparatively more.
(iv) The life of a diesel power plant is small due to high maintenance.
(v) Noise is a serious problem in diesel power plants.
(vi) Diesel power plants cannot be constructed for large scale.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) With the aid of a neat schematic layout diagram, explain the general arrangement and working of a complete Diesel Power Plant. (8 marks)
(b) Explain in detail the Fuel Supply and Handling System from storage tank to engine cylinder. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) General Arrangement and Working of a Diesel Power Plant:

1. Layout and Working Flow:
- When the diesel fuel burns inside the engine cylinder, it starts to produce mechanical power.
- The combustion of fuel produces increased temperature (1500°C to 2000°C) and pressure inside the engine.
- Due to this pressure, expanding gases push the piston inside the diesel engine, producing mechanical power that rotates the crankshaft.
- The rotating shaft directly drives the AC synchronous generator (alternator) to produce electricity.
- The five auxiliary circuits work continuously:
  (i) Air intake system filters incoming ambient air.
  (ii) Fuel supply system feeds metered diesel to injectors.
  (iii) Cooling system circulates water to keep cylinder temperatures within limits.
  (iv) Lubricating system circulates oil to reduce wear and cool parts.
  (v) Exhaust system discharges gases through a silencer.

(b) Fuel Supply System:
(i) Fuel from the outdoor bulk storage tank is pumped through a filter into the all-day tank.
(ii) The all-day tank supplies the daily requirements of the diesel engine by gravity head.
(iii) A fuel overflow pipe returns any excess pumped fuel back to the bulk storage tank.
(iv) Fuel flows from the day tank through secondary fine filters to the high-pressure fuel injection pump and fuel injectors, atomizing fuel into the engine cylinders.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain in detail the Cooling System of a diesel power plant with the help of a flow circuit diagram. (8 marks)
(b) Explain why the cooling water requirement of a diesel power plant is considerably less than that of an equivalent steam power plant. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Cooling System of a Diesel Power Plant:

1. Temperature Conditions and Necessity:
- The temperature of the burning fuel inside the engine cylinder is 1500°C to 2000°C.
- In order to lower this temperature and prevent thermal seizure, water is circulated around the engine.

2. Dual-Circuit Operation:
(i) Jacket Water Circuit: Soft water is circulated through cylinder jackets by a circulating pump, absorbing engine heat. An expansion surge tank maintains positive suction head and accommodates volume changes.
(ii) Heat Exchanger: The hot water leaving the engine jacket is passed through the heat exchanger tubes.
(iii) Raw Water Circuit & Cooling Tower: The heat from the heat exchanger is carried away by raw water circulated through the heat exchanger and is cooled in the cooling tower for recirculation.

(b) Comparison of Cooling Water Requirements:
(i) In a steam power plant, a massive surface condenser is required to condense the entire turbine exhaust steam, requiring huge volumes of cooling water to extract latent heat.
(ii) In a diesel power plant, there is no steam condenser. Heat is carried away primarily by exhaust gases (~30-35%) and shaft work (~35-40%), with only jacket cooling water (~25-30%) needed.
(iii) Hence, diesel power plants have a limited cooling water requirement compared to steam stations.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Describe the Lubricating System of a diesel power plant, explaining the function of each component in the lubrication circuit. (6 marks)
(b) Describe the Air Intake System and Exhaust System used in industrial diesel generating sets. (6 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Lubricating System of a Diesel Power Plant:
(i) Circuit Components: This circuit includes lubricating oil tank, oil pump, and oil cooler.
(ii) Primary Function: The purpose of the lubrication system is to reduce the wear of engine moving parts (parts of the cylinder such as piston, shafts, and valves must be lubricated).
(iii) Cooling Function: Lubrication also helps to cool the engine by taking away frictional heat from bearings and piston walls.
(iv) Oil Cooler: The hot oil returning from the engine is cooled in a water-cooled oil cooler before being pumped back to the lubricating oil tank.

(b) Air Intake System & Exhaust System:
(i) Air Intake System:
  • The air required for the combustion of fuel inside the diesel engine cylinder is drawn through the air filter.
  • The purpose of the filter is to remove dust from the incoming air, protecting precision engine components from abrasive damage.
(ii) Exhaust System:
  • The exhaust gases coming out of the engine are very noisy.
  • In order to reduce the noise, a silencer is used in the exhaust line to dampen exhaust pressure pulsations before discharging flue gases into the atmosphere.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) State the complete list of Advantages and Disadvantages of a Diesel Power Plant. (8 marks)
(b) Explain the practical operating applications and roles of diesel power stations. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Advantages and Disadvantages of Diesel Power Plant:

Advantages:
(i) Very simple design, also simple installation and occupies less space.
(ii) Limited cooling water requirement.
(iii) Diesel power plants are more efficient than steam power in the range of 150 MW capacity.
(iv) Quickly started and put on load.
(v) It can respond to varying loads without any difficulty.
(vi) Smaller storage is needed for the fuel.
(vii) Layout of power plant is quite simple.
(viii) There is no problem of ash handling.
(ix) Less supervision required.

Disadvantages:
(i) High maintenance, lubrication cost, and operating cost.
(ii) Fuel cost is more, since in India diesel is costly.
(iii) The plant cost per kW is comparatively more.
(iv) The life of a diesel power plant is small due to high maintenance.
(v) Noise is a serious problem in diesel power plants.
(vi) Diesel power plants cannot be constructed for large scale.

(b) Operating Applications and Roles:
(i) Peak Load Plant: Operated during peak demand hours due to fast starting ability (within 2 to 5 minutes).
(ii) Standby / Emergency Power Station: Installed in hospitals, data centers, airports, and industrial plants during main grid failure.
(iii) Remote / Isolated Grids: Deployed on islands, hill stations, and remote mines where high-voltage transmission lines are uneconomical.
(iv) Nursery Station: Installed in newly developing areas to supply local load until bulk power grid lines are extended.
